rv.q: "A whirlwind of highbrow showmanship. But what keeps it from being pretentious is the sincere explosive joy with which it’s constructed...Stoppard’s writing is generous in its virtuosity...
You’re never going to see a finer revival of “Travesties,” so catch this one while you can.
What emerges from the churning wash of “Travesties” is one of the sweetest, sauciest and strangest defenses of art ever to land on a stage.
Fun on its own etymological terms, this madcap comedy also tips its hat — a beat-up straw boater with a jaunty red hatband — to the spirit of revolution that galvanized Europe in 1917.
Tom Hollander's performance as Henry Carr is a marvel of precision and comic timing, anchoring this brilliant revival
Sparkling and incisive revival...continues to illuminate our untethered times with whiplash accuracy.
Only a playwright as brilliantly inventive as Stoppard could put all that together to come up with an uproarious work that seriously questions the nature of art.

Under Marber’s careful direction, Hollander takes Stoppard’s comically befuddled British consul into some unforeseen emotional terrain, never more moving than when Carr recalls the horror of the trenches and the patriotism of its fighters. If Hollander’s Carr can’t quite sway the cynical Tzara – and he can’t – no one can.
Washington’s arrival is an electrifying pinnacle of this elliptical, marathon play, which in this outing clocks in at almost four hours.
This production does it proud, with Patrick Marber's direction finding the right balance.
Tom Hollander gives a tour de force performance as Henry Carr in this witty revival that makes Stoppard's intellectual comedy feel surprisingly accessible and entertaining.

"You don't have to enroll for a graduate degree to enjoy Stoppard's simultaneously wacky and intellectual comedy..That's largely due to the accessible nature of Marber's rollickingly staged production...The plot is nothing more than a springboard for the playwright's unique brand of clever wordplay and cerebral observations...
If you're looking for an example of theatrical brilliance made tangible, here's what you do.
Even if you can't solve it all as you watch, it's a pleasure to engage with a production that does Travesties full justice.
In fact, most of “Travesties” will leave you with a wide grin on your mouth, while still providing fodder for your brain.
For a Stoppard fan, it’s a delight: so rich, so dense, so silly, and paced so superbly by Marber and a uniformly excellent cast that you hardly realize how very much information is packed in.
Revival of Tom Stoppard's Travesties is a giddy, head-spinning triumph
If I had to name the liveliest, most inventive and well worth seeing plays of the current Theater season, the revival of Stoppard's 'Travesties' would make my top three.
This is still one of the playwright's most impressive achievements.

Luckily, the first Broadway revival of Stoppard’s 1974 play turns this challenging exercise in virtuosity into an often-hilarious entertainment, with lively direction by Patrick Marber and a spot-on eight-member cast led by the terrific Tom Hollander.
For what it's worth, you have my blessing to rest your mind at various intervals, because no matter where you rejoin, there will be some bit of awesome insanity to keep your head in an endless spin.
Under Patrick Marber's masterful direction, 'Travesties' never lets the mayhem swirl completely out of control.
Broadway’s spry revival of “Travesties” is guaranteed to work your gray matter.
Stoppard’s genius, especially in his earlier work, is to mix high intellect with low comedy, and Travesties manages to be both deeply thoughtful and guffawingly funny.
A challenging comedy of ideas on art, politics and memory, Travesties will prove caviar to the general but intoxicating theater for those who are disposed to its intricacies.
The drama becomes blunted when it feels as if we are being shouted at; the stage of the Lucille Lortel feels too small for it.
It is hard to imagine a better production of it coming along anytime soon, and how do you get to complain about a play being too smart?
But these multi-talented thespians do it with such zesty effortlessness, they make it all seem like so much fun.
Arguably the best and smartest play on Broadway right now, and a must see for any serious theatregoer.
This pitch-perfectly acted version manages the rare feat of being both intellectually stimulating, visually appealing, and hilariously funny.
So go forth, dive in, read up, or not, as you’ll enjoy every drop regardless of how you enter.
I did not expect to be so delighted by this rollicking production imported by Roundabout Theatre from London’s Menier Chocolate Factory.
Travesties demands attention from its audience as it challenges our intellect -- but it moves quickly and intelligently so there’s no dozing off.
I didn't care because the tremendously talented Tom Hollander plays Henry Carr and he is amazing!
A rollicking good time with an intellectual perspective wrapped in theater of the absurd.
The crossfire is blisteringly bizarre and oftentimes incomprehensible.
Those who are willing to focus on the rapid fire, complex dialog will be delighted by the delivery.

cn.t: Critics hail this "dazzling" and "sparkling" revival of Stoppard's intellectually dense 1974 comedy, praising Marber's inventive direction and Hollander's brilliant performance, though some find the verbal pyrotechnics exhausting or overly cerebral.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
